strengths: Soundness: The main continuous-time analysis provides a useful conditional Wasserstein bound. The proof connects OU regularization, log-Sobolev inequalities, inexact Langevin convergence, and reverse-ODE stability, with explicit contributions from early stopping, score error, and initialization error.

Originality: Theorem 4.2 is the most distinctive contribution. Its score-confinement argument and clipping construction convert terminal L2 error into the exponential-moment control needed by the Langevin analysis. This supplies new understanding beyond simply applying an existing predictor-corrector sampler.

Significance: Keeping the forward horizon independent of the desired sampling accuracy is a meaningful theoretical advance relative to the cited Wasserstein analysis. The norm-subgaussian assumption covers a broad class of targets without requiring the original distribution to satisfy a functional inequality.

Presentation and reproducibility: The error decomposition and proof roadmap are clear, and Appendices A–C provide substantial detail for checking the mathematics. Section 6 explicitly acknowledges the missing reverse-ODE discretization analysis. The theoretical work and synthetic examples raise no apparent material research-ethics concerns.
weaknesses: The claim of convergence from the standard integrated L2 training loss needs qualification. Theorem 4.2 requires separate control of b(T1), which does not follow from J_SM tending to zero under A1: an error concentrated in a shrinking time interval near T1 can retain a fixed terminal error. Moreover, the stability factor I_tau depends exponentially on the estimator's one-sided Lipschitz constants; the additional condition discussed on page 7 is not implied by small training loss. An explicit combined corollary should state all these requirements.

The computational improvement remains incomplete. Proposition 6.1 establishes the stated O(epsilon^-2 log(1/epsilon)) complexity only for sampling p_T1, before reverse propagation and ODE discretization. Section 6 honestly identifies this limitation, but its comparison with complete diffusion samplers does not establish an overall speedup. Likewise, the logarithmic dependence concerns the required forward horizon; the full error and complexity bounds also contain dimension-dependent early-stopping, stability, and discretization terms.

Several mathematical statements need correction. Equations (3.3) and (3.5) have coefficients inconsistent with (3.1)–(3.2): the conventional parameterization requires score coefficient M g^2/2 and diffusion coefficient sqrt(M-1) g. Also, the final sufficient condition in Lemma 5.6 is false as written: for d=1, p concentrated at sqrt(2/3), and t=log(sqrt(2)), its condition holds but KL(gamma || p_t) is approximately 0.487, exceeding 1/3. These appear repairable without changing the core OU argument.

The numerical evidence is not reproducible from the manuscript. Figure 1 omits the fixed T1 values, score-model and training details, numerical solvers and step sizes, sample counts, Wasserstein estimation procedure, and meaning of the error bars. No implementation is supplied. Decreasing Wasserstein error on three toy examples also does not establish the accompanying claim that the exponential-moment loss is small without clipping.

The originality assessment is limited by the literature coverage. The comparisons stop at 2023; an ICML 2026 submission needs to establish how these guarantees relate to subsequent probability-flow ODE and predictor-corrector convergence results.
